questions.stem: In this anterior view of the sternum and thoracic skeleton, the palpable ridge between the manubrium and the body is an important surface landmark. The rib that articulates at this ridge marks the level of which structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The xiphisternal joint and the diaphragm dome

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fifth rib and the cardiac apex

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second costal cartilage, used to start counting ribs; it also marks the T4/T5 disc level

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first rib and the apex of the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: The clavicle and the subclavian vein

explanation.summary: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum and marks the joint of the second costal cartilage, the reference point for counting ribs. Internally it lies at the T4/T5 intervertebral disc, the level of the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation (carina).
explanation.whyCorrect: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum and marks the joint of the second costal cartilage, the reference point for counting ribs. Internally it lies at the T4/T5 intervertebral disc, the level of the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation (carina).

questions.stem: This diagram shows the intercostal neurovascular bundle running in the costal groove on the underside of a rib. To avoid injuring this bundle during a thoracocentesis, where should the needle be inserted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Directly along the lower border of the rib above

choices.label: B
choices.text: As close as possible to the vertebral end of the rib

choices.label: C
choices.text: Through the middle of the intercostal space at the costal groove

choices.label: D
choices.text: Just above the upper border of the rib below the target space

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immediately deep to the internal thoracic vessels near the sternum

explanation.summary: The vein, artery and nerve (VAN, superior to inferior) run in the costal groove tucked beneath the lower border of each rib. Inserting the needle just over the top of the rib below the space keeps it away from the main bundle, minimizing the risk of neurovascular injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vein, artery and nerve (VAN, superior to inferior) run in the costal groove tucked beneath the lower border of each rib. Inserting the needle just over the top of the rib below the space keeps it away from the main bundle, minimizing the risk of neurovascular injury.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This figure labels the muscles associated with breathing. Which of these is the principal muscle responsible for quiet (resting) inspiration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rectus abdominis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The external obliques

choices.label: C
choices.text: The internal intercostals

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sternocleidomastoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The diaphragm

explanation.summary: The diaphragm performs most of the work of quiet inspiration; its contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume. The scalenes and external intercostals assist, while sternocleidomastoid and other accessory muscles are recruited only in forced inspiration. Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diaphragm performs most of the work of quiet inspiration; its contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume. The scalenes and external intercostals assist, while sternocleidomastoid and other accessory muscles are recruited only in forced inspiration. Abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This cutaway shows the three layers of intercostal muscle between two ribs. The outermost of these layers, with fibers running downward and forward, has what primary action in breathing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It elevates the ribs to increase thoracic volume during inspiration

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depresses the ribs during forced expiration

choices.label: C
choices.text: It compresses the abdominal contents during coughing

choices.label: D
choices.text: It flattens the diaphragm dome directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: It has no role in ventilation and only stabilizes the spine

explanation.summary: The external intercostal muscles have fibers oriented obliquely downward and forward and act to elevate the ribs, aiding inspiration. The internal and innermost intercostals, with fibers running the opposite way, pull the ribs down and assist forced expiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The external intercostal muscles have fibers oriented obliquely downward and forward and act to elevate the ribs, aiding inspiration. The internal and innermost intercostals, with fibers running the opposite way, pull the ribs down and assist forced expiration.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This dissection of the anterior thoracic wall highlights the segmental nerves (yellow/green) running along the ribs. These nerves that supply the intercostal spaces and thoracic wall are the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cervical plexus nerves C1-C4

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thoracic spinal nerves T1-T11 (the intercostal nerves)

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrenic nerve from C3-C5

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lumbar plexus nerves L1-L4

explanation.summary: The anterior rami of T1-T11 form the intercostal nerves, which run in the costal grooves with the intercostal vessels and supply the intercostal muscles and overlying skin. The T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve. These are distinct from the phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anterior rami of T1-T11 form the intercostal nerves, which run in the costal grooves with the intercostal vessels and supply the intercostal muscles and overlying skin. The T12 anterior ramus is the subcostal nerve. These are distinct from the phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This figure shows the lungs within the rib cage and the pleural recesses at the lung bases. The costodiaphragmatic recess has what important clinical significance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is normally completely filled by lung at all times

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the most dependent part of the pleural cavity where fluid collects and where thoracentesis is performed

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is where the trachea bifurcates into main bronchi

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the site where the phrenic nerve enters the diaphragm

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the location of the cardiac notch of the left lung

explanation.summary: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the deep pleural gutter between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura that lung tissue only fills during deep inspiration. As the most dependent recess, it is where a pleural effusion first accumulates and is the target for thoracentesis, typically entered in the mid-to-posterior axillary line.
explanation.whyCorrect: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the deep pleural gutter between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura that lung tissue only fills during deep inspiration. As the most dependent recess, it is where a pleural effusion first accumulates and is the target for thoracentesis, typically entered in the mid-to-posterior axillary line.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This anterior view of the diaphragm shows its right and left domes. Why does the right dome (right hemidiaphragm) normally sit higher than the left?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heart rests on the right dome and depresses the left

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right lung is larger and compresses its dome down

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stomach lies under the right dome and elevates it

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bulk of the liver lies beneath the right dome and pushes it upward

choices.label: E
choices.text: The right crus is shorter than the left crus

explanation.summary: The large right lobe of the liver sits directly under the right hemidiaphragm and pushes it about one intercostal space higher than the left. The left dome is slightly lower partly because of the underlying stomach and the heart resting on it. This is a normal finding on chest imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: The large right lobe of the liver sits directly under the right hemidiaphragm and pushes it about one intercostal space higher than the left. The left dome is slightly lower partly because of the underlying stomach and the heart resting on it. This is a normal finding on chest imaging.

questions.stem: This inferior view of the diaphragm shows the openings for the inferior vena cava, esophagus, and aorta. At which vertebral level does the esophageal hiatus (esophagus opening) lie?

choices.label: A
choices.text: L1

choices.label: D
choices.text: T6

choices.label: E
choices.text: T8

explanation.summary: The caval opening is at T8, the esophageal hiatus at T10, and the aortic hiatus at T12. Recalling '8-10-12' (vena cava, esophagus/vagus, aorta) links each structure to its level.
explanation.whyCorrect: The caval opening is at T8, the esophageal hiatus at T10, and the aortic hiatus at T12. Recalling '8-10-12' (vena cava, esophagus/vagus, aorta) links each structure to its level.

questions.stem: The nerve highlighted in yellow running along the pericardium to the diaphragm provides what functional supply?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parasympathetic supply to abdominal viscera

choices.label: B
choices.text: Motor supply to the intercostal muscles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sensory supply to the lung parenchyma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sympathetic supply to the heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Motor innervation to the diaphragm

explanation.summary: The phrenic nerve descends alongside the pericardium and provides the sole motor innervation to the diaphragm (plus sensory fibers to the pericardium and central diaphragm).
explanation.whyCorrect: The phrenic nerve descends alongside the pericardium and provides the sole motor innervation to the diaphragm (plus sensory fibers to the pericardium and central diaphragm).

questions.stem: The nerve shown branching over the diaphragm (sternal, anterolateral, and posterior branches) arises from which spinal roots?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C1-C3

choices.label: B
choices.text: L1-L2

choices.label: C
choices.text: T1-T4

choices.label: E
choices.text: C3-C5

explanation.summary: The phrenic nerve arises from cervical roots C3, C4, and C5 ('C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive'), then fans into terminal branches on the diaphragm's inferior surface.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phrenic nerve arises from cervical roots C3, C4, and C5 ('C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive'), then fans into terminal branches on the diaphragm's inferior surface.

questions.stem: The right panel is a normal frontal chest radiograph with the posterior ribs numbered. Counting posterior ribs visible above the diaphragm is used clinically to judge what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The degree of rotation of the film

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adequacy of inspiratory effort (degree of lung inflation)

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presence of a rib fracture

choices.label: D
choices.text: The size of the cardiac silhouette

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's total blood volume

explanation.summary: On a well-inspired PA chest film, roughly 9-10 posterior ribs (or 5-6 anterior ribs) should be visible above the diaphragm. Fewer ribs suggests a poor inspiratory effort, which can mimic or obscure pathology such as basal atelectasis or increased lung markings.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a well-inspired PA chest film, roughly 9-10 posterior ribs (or 5-6 anterior ribs) should be visible above the diaphragm. Fewer ribs suggests a poor inspiratory effort, which can mimic or obscure pathology such as basal atelectasis or increased lung markings.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This figure separates the muscles of inspiration from the muscles of expiration. During QUIET (resting) breathing, expiration is accomplished mainly by which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall, with no active muscle contraction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of the diaphragm pushing air out

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forceful contraction of the internal intercostals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contraction of the scalenes and sternocleidomastoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contraction of the rectus abdominis and external obliques

explanation.summary: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the stored elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall drives air out. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals shown here are recruited only for active, forced expiration such as coughing or exercise.
explanation.whyCorrect: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the stored elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall drives air out. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals shown here are recruited only for active, forced expiration such as coughing or exercise.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Diaphragm, Ribs, and Intercostal Muscles
questions.stem: This figure contrasts the chest and diaphragm during breathing in versus breathing out. During inspiration, how does diaphragm contraction change intrathoracic pressure and drive airflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relaxes and ascends, pulling air into the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: It domes upward, decreasing thoracic volume and pushing air in

choices.label: C
choices.text: It flattens and descends, increasing thoracic volume and lowering intrapleural/alveolar pressure so air flows in

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises alveolar pressure above atmospheric, drawing air in

choices.label: E
choices.text: It has no effect on volume; only the ribs move air

explanation.summary: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.
